newsitem.title: VATICAN: Vatican, Vietnam resume dialogue amid difficulties.
newsitem.headline: Vatican, Vietnam resume dialogue amid difficulties.

text.p: The Vatican and Vietnam's communist government have resumed a "frank and respectful" dialogue after a frosty 18-month break, a Vatican official said on Friday.
"After a year and a half, the Holy See and the Hanoi government have resumed a dialogue in frankness and with mutual respect," Archbishop Claudio Maria Celli said.

Hanoi has eased tight controls on religious freedoms in recent years, but relations with the Holy See have floundered over a range of differences, some of which, including the naming of bishops, are fundamental.

Celli, who led a delegation that visited the country last week, told Vatican Radio he had told the government that the Roman Catholic Church wanted to be allowed to help more in education, health and agriculture.
Celli, a former diplomat who is the Vatican's expert on Vietnam, said the communist government expressed interest in Church initiatives as long as they had no ulterior motives.
He said the Vatican and Vietnam were still "on different wavelengths" on the issue of religious freedom.
The prelate said that while places of worship were open and the minority Catholic population was allowed to attend mass, the Catholic Church was up against "not a few limitations".
The Vietnamese government had, however, given its approval for the appointment of two assistant bishops in Ho Chi Minh City.
"This is a small but positive step on a difficult road," Celli said.
During the visit, the government told the delegation that it was not interested in help from foreign organisations or countries if there were strings attached.
Most of Vietnam's 75 million population is Buddhist, but its estimated seven million Catholic community is one of the largest in East Asia.
